_help: THE voices for every @maddiee.makess reel (Option 3 (American teen Maddie + young British Claude), re-chosen 2026-11-11). Never change the refs: every line is cloned from them so Maddie and Claude always sound the same. Per reel: copy this file to studio/voices/<scene>.json, fill 'jobs' (one per line, emotion tags like [sigh] [laughter] [surprise-oh] [surprise-wa] [question-en] [dissatisfaction-hnn] go inside the text), run the 'voices (OmniVoice)' workflow with that config, then put the wavs in codevid/voice/<scene>/NN.wav (render.js uses them automatically).

ref_text.maddie: Claude, I graduated today. Zero offers. So I'm going back. Master's. Stanford.
ref_text.claude: Okay. Give me your resume. Step one. Connect Playwright. Free, made by Microsoft. Two hundred career pages.

jobs.text: Claude, why is there a big X on the last coach of every train?
It's not decoration. It's a safety check.
When a train passes a station, the station master looks for that X.
Why? To say bye?
To make sure the whole train arrived. No coaches left behind.
Coaches can get left behind?!
If a coupling breaks, the last coaches can detach and stop right on the track.
No X means a missing piece. The next train is stopped before it hits them.
Wait... so one letter stops a crash?
Yes. In the day there's also an L V board. Last Vehicle. At night, a blinking red lamp.
And I thought it was just for style.
Send this to the friend who always takes the window in sleeper class.
Claude! I looked away for five seconds and the milk exploded!
Classic. Water never does that. Milk does.
Why though? Now I have to clean all this.
When milk heats up, its proteins and fat float up and form a thin skin on top.
In water, bubbles reach the top and just pop.
But milk bubbles hit that skin... and get trapped.
So they pile up?
More and more steam pushes the skin up like a lid. Then whoosh. All over the stove.
How do I stop it?
Lower the flame and keep stirring. That breaks the skin, so the steam can escape.
So the skin was the villain all along.
Send this to the friend whose chai always boils over.
Claude, why do biscuits have these tiny holes? Is it just design?
Nope. Those holes are there because of the oven.
Biscuit dough has water in it. In the oven, that water turns into steam.
Okay... so?
Steam needs a way out. With no holes, it gets trapped inside.
The biscuit puffs up like a balloon, bakes uneven, and cracks.
Wait. So the holes are tiny chimneys?
Exactly. Steam slips out through them, and the biscuit stays flat and crisp.
Bakers even have a name for it. It's called docking.
My whole childhood... I was eating chimneys.
Send this to the friend who dips every biscuit in chai.
Claude, why do our notes have these little lines on the sides?
Close your eyes. Now touch them.
Wait... they're raised?
Yes. They're for people who can't see.
Count them. The hundred rupee note has four. The five hundred has five.
So you can tell the note just by touch?!
Yes. There's also a raised mark to feel, and every note is a different size.
My wallet had a secret code this whole time.
Next time you get a note, close your eyes and feel the edges.
Send this to someone who still counts money twice.
Claude, why can't we use phones at petrol pumps? Will it really blast?
Here's the twist. Experts have never found a single fire caused by a phone.
What?! Then why the board?
Partly an old rumour. And partly because a phone distracts you near fuel.
The real danger is something smaller. Static electricity.
Static? Like the shock from a door handle?
Exactly. Petrol gives off vapour. One tiny spark from your body can light it.
Most of these fires happened when people got back into the car while filling, then touched the nozzle.
So the phone was innocent this whole time.
Mostly. But still follow the board at the pump. And never smoke there.
Send this to the friend who always says, phone off bro, it'll blast.
